newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy markets rise on lira/ERM then slump on Prodi.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy markets rise on lira/ERM then slump on Prodi.

text.p: Italian stocks and bond futures rose on Monday after the lira's return to the European currency grid after four years' absence -- only to slump on reports of judicial problems for Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
After 17 hours of talks at the weekend European Union ministers finally agreed on a central rate of 990 per mark for the lira to rejoin the exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
"No-one's screaming buy the market, but the ERM return marks the beginning of something which could be quite positive for Italy," said Oriano Moro, trader at Gestnord brokers here.
"It's like passing your driving test. Now we've got our licence let's see if we can actually drive," Moro added.

The all-share Mibtel index put on 0.7 percent in early trade but reversed gear and fell by 0.94 percent on reports a Rome magistrate had asked for Prodi to be charged with abuse of office when he headed state industrial holding IRI in 1993.
Italian Btp bond futures, which hit new historic highs in morning trade, also retreated on the reports.
The lira, after a high of 990.15 per mark, slipped after the report on Prodi but then recovered near to the day's highs.
"As far as Prodi is concerned, we're waiting for further information -- it had a bad impact but the market's stable now," one broker at a Milan stockbrokers said.
Moro pointed out markets had widely expected the lira to return to the ERM over the weekend after it was cast out in a currency crisis in September 1992.
"There's no euphoria with people saying the future's rosy now we're back in. The market looks slightly overbought technically and some consolidation is expected," he said.
Luca Jellinek, bond strategist at Paribas in London, said domestic investors considered the lira's return "a good thing".
"They're not looking too closely at the details and the fact that the French and Germans played hard ball, which isn't too good for EMU," he said.
Italy was readmitted to the grid at a stronger level than the 1,010 Rome had wanted and one agreed after hours of tough negotiations with other EU partners, most notably Germany.

Marco Nascimbeni, head of operations at Carnegie Italia brokers, said the stock market was very quiet. "What is stopping stocks from rallying is the perception that some investors are taking their profits from some export-oriented companies.
"Some wanted to see lira back in ERM at over 1,000. We think 990 is reasonable, the difference is negligible. The result is all about giving a good message to our partners," he said.
Nascimbeni also said the future reaction of the stock market was tied to developments on the 1997 budget bill which he saw being finally approved in parliament in the next 10 to 14 days.
Italian investors remained optimistic about the prospects for stocks and foreign investors were looking for the right time to return to the Italian market, he said.
Moro referred to the centre-left government's keenness to whip Italy into economic shape in time for the start of a European single currency in 1999.

"The market feeling is that Prodi's government is trying to achieve something whether it's correct or not. Some fiscal aspects of the budget are not being taken well in the country, but an international investor is not concerned about domestic issues - he's looking to see what he can get out of the market."
